Winning the Pre-Seed Without a Product — TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 panel

Source: TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 panel, YouTube BzZtbLGGwUs (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BzZtbLGGwUs). Transcript pulled 2026-10-19 via research-kit. Speakers (names garbled in the captions; firms inferred from what they say on stage, so treat as unverified): - "Sandhya": founder of Axiom, a first-time ~$50–100M AI fund. Backed Fourth Thought AI (Battlefield 2018). - "Rohit": early-stage firm that writes $1–5M first checks. Cites Fitbit ($1.75M first check, largest holder through IPO) and Duo Security (Michigan). Both fit True Ventures. - "Austin": firm whose internal motto he gives as "your life experience is your competitive advantage." Runs a Friends & Family accelerator. Wrote a $3M check to a solo nuclear-reactor founder a week after the founder quit their job. Courses mapped: Course 10 (Entrepreneurship & Venture), E7 (Executive Presence & Comms), E8 (Investor Relations). Bias line: a conference stage where the speakers are recruiting deal flow. Every example is a winner they backed (survivorship). The captions read like a machine back-translation ("pre-sowing stage"), so wording is approximate. Paraphrased here, with no verbatim quotes.

Core claim

At pre-seed the bet is placed on the founder's non-obvious vision and their ability to tell it, not on traction. Cheap AI prototypes have raised the bar: everyone can now show a demo, so a demo has stopped being a signal.

Framework: what they actually screen for

Signal What it looks like Who stressed it
Founder–market fit + unique insight A domain résumé is table stakes. The edge is the intersection of domain experience with an unusual second experience, which yields a view "five smart people in a room" wouldn't reach All three
"Born to win," not "right to win" Obsession that shows even in conversation. Not an incubator founder hunting for an idea Sandhya
Asymmetric thinking Founders who look for deviations, never averages. They make you see a market that doesn't exist yet (Fitbit's brick-with-AA-batteries prototype) Rohit
Customer contact before product "Who is the customer, how well do you know them, how will you reach them?" comes before the demo Rohit
Talent magnetism People quitting a strong company to follow you is the strongest pre-product green flag Austin
Two-register communication Can go deep technically and explain it to a layperson. The same skill drives hiring, fundraising and press Austin, Sandhya
"Why you win" over "moat" Moat is overrated at pre-seed. Answer why you beat five equally smart teams who reach the same conclusion Sandhya
Venture scale "$10M revenue potential" isn't a venture case Sandhya

Red flags

  • AI-written cold outreach. Spotted within a couple of words. "You invested in X, so look at us" is not an argument.
  • No path to a warm intro. Not a judgment outsourced to the referrer. The point is that failing to find one is an "invisible" negative signal. Network angle: the firm's portfolio founders and employees count as paths in.
  • Not knowing your competitive set, including anything that competes for the customer's money or time. If the VC names a competitor you haven't heard of, that's a flag.
  • Fundraising aversion. "I want to get this over with so I can get back to the business" tells the VC you don't see capital-raising as part of the CEO job. Sandhya's own arc as a first-time GP shows this mindset is fixable.
  • "Show more traction" is a coded message. It means some part of your story isn't believed. It's not a fixed metrics threshold.

Relationship tactics

  • Open with "we're not raising right now." It makes the conversation non-transactional and unlocks candid feedback. VCs give feedback only when asked.
  • Treat the lead as a 7–10-year board relationship. The scarce resource is founder time, not money.
  • The 9pm test: can you text your first investor at night and get an answer in about 15 minutes?
  • Geography: not a constraint for these three (Duo/Michigan; board seats in Zurich and Helsinki).

Applies when

  • Deep-tech, AI or new-category bets where no traction is possible yet, and a lead underwrites the team at $1–5M.
  • The founder has a real, explainable experience asymmetry.

Breaks when

  • The warm-intro filter hits founders without networks. The panel conceded this (women and founders of color get "advice instead of money") and estimated 10–100 missed deals a year. Sandhya pushed back with a "no excuses" story: three months of grinding every contact from her career. Both are true. The filter is a bug the firms profit from tolerating.
  • "Born to win" and "I can feel the passion over a few dinners" are unfalsifiable, so pattern-matching bias gets in. Compare with canon kahneman thinking fast and slow-style intuition-validity conditions: the feedback loop runs 7–10 years and is survivorship-filtered.
  • Competitor overfunding (an audience question: a rival raised $30M at $100M pre-launch). The panel's answer: it doesn't set your valuation, it raises your burden of proof. That's dodgy advice for hardware, where capital is the moat.

Practitioner counterpoint

  • harlem capital vc insights: says to engineer warm intros (pre-built target lists, 2–3 specific asks). That's the tactical answer to this panel's structural complaint.
  • primary venture partners insights: scaled-seed firms industrialize sourcing (BDRs, talent teams). That works against the "only via network" claim and suggests cold inbound is becoming more viable at large seed platforms.
  • entrepreneurship operator playbook: "between-rounds death." The panel's "you'll need $200M before product" remark is the extreme case. Size the pre-seed to reach a fundable milestone, not a demo.
  • tiger sisters private capital 101: the VC-as-clubby framing, confirmed here from the inside.

Retrieval prompts

  1. Why does a cheap AI MVP raise rather than lower the pre-seed bar?
  2. Distinguish "right to win," "born to win," and "moat." Which one do pre-seed investors weight, and why?
  3. A VC says "we'd love to see more traction." What does it actually mean, and what should you change?
  4. Give two reasons the warm-intro requirement persists, and one way it degrades the VC's own returns.
